meta.title: Angry or Compassionate?
meta.subtitle: The text of Mark 1:41 — witnesses, transmission models, arguments
meta.lede: When the leper says “If you will, you can make me clean”, almost every manuscript says Jesus was moved with compassion (σπλαγχνισθείς). Codex Bezae and a handful of Latin manuscripts say he became angry (ὀργισθείς). Most commentators think anger is original; most critical editions print compassion. This page lays out the evidence and the arguments so the reasoning can be traced step by step.

verses.greek: Καὶ ἔρχεται πρὸς αὐτὸν λεπρὸς παρακαλῶν αὐτὸν [καὶ γονυπετῶν] καὶ λέγων αὐτῷ ὅτι ἐὰν θέλῃς δύνασαί με καθαρίσαι.
verses.english: A leper comes to him, begging him [and kneeling] and saying to him, “If you will, you can make me clean.”

verses.greek: καὶ {σπλαγχνισθεὶς | ὀργισθεὶς} ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ἥψατο καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· θέλω, καθαρίσθητι·
verses.english: And {moved with compassion | becoming angry}, he stretched out his hand and touched him and says to him, “I will; be clean.”

verses.greek: καὶ εὐθὺς ἀπῆλθεν ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἡ λέπρα, καὶ ἐκαθαρίσθη.
verses.english: And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.

verses.greek: καὶ ἐμβριμησάμενος αὐτῷ εὐθὺς ἐξέβαλεν αὐτόν
verses.english: And sternly warning him (lit. “snorting at him”), he immediately drove him out
verses.note: ἐμβριμησάμενος and ἐξέβαλεν are the harsh words that figure in every argument below.

verses.greek: καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· ὅρα μηδενὶ μηδὲν εἴπῃς, ἀλλ᾿ ὕπαγε σεαυτὸν δεῖξον τῷ ἱερεῖ καὶ προσένεγκε περὶ τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ σου ἃ προσέταξεν Μωϋσῆς, εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς.
verses.english: and says to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone; but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

verses.greek: Ὁ δὲ ἐξελθὼν ἤρξατο κηρύσσειν πολλὰ καὶ διαφημίζειν τὸν λόγον, ὥστε μηκέτι αὐτὸν δύνασθαι φανερῶς εἰς πόλιν εἰσελθεῖν, ἀλλ᾿ ἔξω ἐπ᾿ ἐρήμοις τόποις ἦν· καὶ ἤρχοντο πρὸς αὐτὸν πάντοθεν.
verses.english: But he went out and began to proclaim it freely and to spread the word, so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly but stayed out in deserted places; and they came to him from everywhere.

howToRead: The first unit concerns only the opening words: most manuscripts read ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς (“But Jesus”), while ℵ B D 892 and the Old Latin read καί (“And”), which NA28 prints.

The second unit is the one at issue. NA28 lists only the witnesses against its text: ὀργισθείς is read by D (Codex Bezae) and the Old Latin manuscripts a, ff² and r¹ (first hand, marked *). Every other witness is implied for σπλαγχνισθείς.
Notice that Bezae sides with ℵ and B in the first unit (καί) and stands alone among Greek manuscripts in the second.

witnesses.summary: No papyrus preserves this verse (P137 covers Mark 1:7–9 and 16–18 only; P45 begins in Mark 4). The earliest Greek evidence is from the fourth century.

count.text: In Text und Textwert, 1623 of 1631 Greek manuscripts read σπλαγχνισθείς at this test passage.

groups.title: Both: compassion and anger
groups.reading: ܐܬܪܚܡ ܥܠܘܗܝ ܘܟܕ ܡܦܪ — “had compassion on him and, being angered, …”

items.name: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on the Gospel Harmony (Diatessaron) XII.21–24
items.attests: “Our Lord was angry, therefore, about both things” … “reproof through his anger, and compassion through his healing” … “again, it is said that he was not angry with him, but with his leprosy.”
items.note: Ephrem explains a text that had both emotions. The key word mpār (“being angered”) was mistranslated in the standard editions (Leloir: succendebat; McCarthy: “was refuting”), so its status as a gospel citation was missed until Taylor 2020.

items.name: Old Syriac Gospels, fragmentary palimpsest (Sinai Syr. NF 37 + NF 39)
items.attests: “Now he, Jesus, had compassion on him and, being angered, stretched out his hand and touched him.”
items.note: The third known Old Syriac gospel manuscript, read by multispectral imaging. Cited in the ECM of Mark as a separate reading together with Ephrem.
items.source: Taylor 2020, p. 22; ECM Mark 1:41/2-10, reading h

items.name: Codex Veronensis
items.note: Read either as discomfort with an inherited iratus or as assimilation to Matthew and Luke.

items.name: Greek minuscules and one lectionary
items.note: 1358 was wrongly listed with Bezae for ὀργισθείς in Text und Textwert (1998); Jeff Cate checked the film in 2011 and found it simply omits the word. The error still circulates.

items.name: Codex Palatinus
items.note: Represents the oldest (African) stratum of the Latin gospels. Codex Bobiensis (k) is lacking here.

items.name: Sinaitic Syriac (Old Syriac)
items.note: The Curetonian Syriac is not extant here.

takeaways: Anger is found in one Greek manuscript and one Latin text-type, centred on northern Italy from about 350.
Around the same time, in Syria, Ephrem is commenting on a text that has both compassion and anger; the same double text survives in an Old Syriac manuscript.
Compassion is read everywhere else, including in the oldest branch of each version where anger appears (African Latin e; Sinaitic Syriac).
So the anger reading is not a quirk of one codex: two unconnected language areas know it by the mid-fourth century.

models.intro: Three accounts of how the tradition came to look this way. Each has to explain the same facts; they differ in where the change happened and in which direction. Select a model to see which witnesses and arguments support it and which strain it.

items.title: Anger is original
items.short: Mark wrote ὀργισθείς; an early correction to σπλαγχνισθείς took over almost everywhere.

nodes.label: Early correction
nodes.note: one pious change, upstream of most later copies

nodes.label: All other Greek lines · African Latin · Sinaitic Syriac · Coptic

explains: Why anyone would change the text: anger with no stated cause is an embarrassment; compassion is the obvious repair.
Why both Matthew and Luke lack any emotion word.
The harsh tone of verse 43 (ἐμβριμησάμενος, ἐξέβαλεν).
Why anger turns up in both Latin and Syriac: both inherit an old Greek text.
costs: The correction must have happened early enough to stand upstream of every other Greek line and of the oldest Latin, Syriac and Coptic branches.
No Greek trace survives outside one bilingual codex whose Greek text is late and mixed at this very verse.
Scribes left Jesus' anger untouched at Mark 3:5 and his indignation at 10:14.

holders.name: C. H. Turner
holders.note: Harder reading; Matthew and Luke drop it as they drop μετ᾿ ὀργῆς (3:5) and ἐμβριμησάμενος.

holders.name: J. K. Elliott
holders.note: The UBS committee “allowed itself to be overwhelmed by the sheer number of MSS”.

holders.name: Morna Hooker
holders.note: “Almost certainly the correct reading.”

holders.name: Mark Proctor
holders.note: Dissertation devoted to the case for an angry Jesus.

holders.name: Joel Marcus
holders.note: σπλαγχνισθείς “is probably a scribal amelioration”.

holders.name: R. T. France
holders.note: “It is hard to see why anyone should introduce ὀργισθείς.”

holders.name: Bart Ehrman
holders.note: Once altered, the change “could easily have spread like wildfire”.

holders.name: H. Greeven & E. Güting
holders.note: Bezae among the witnesses preserving the ancient text here.

holders.name: M. Eugene Boring
holders.note: “A change from ‘being angry’ to ‘having compassion’ is readily explained, but not vice versa.”

holders.name: Michael Holmes (SBLGNT)
holders.note: Prints ὀργισθείς.

holders.name: NIV committee
holders.note: “Jesus was indignant.”

holders.name: Jean-Claude Haelewyck
holders.note: Variant of this model: three successive editions of the pericope, Bezae's (anger throughout) the earliest.

holders.name: Bart Bruehler
holders.note: Most recent defence of the anger reading.

variants.title: Lake's twist (1923)
variants.text: ὀργισθείς is original, but its subject is the leper, who touches Jesus “in a passion of rage”. Rejected by France (“an exegetical counsel of despair”) and Collins.

items.title: Compassion is original; anger is an early Greek variant
items.short: Mark wrote σπλαγχνισθείς; ὀργισθείς arose once, in the second century, in a “Western” Greek text.

nodes.label: Matthew, Luke
nodes.note: abbreviate; Matthew reuses the word at 20:34

nodes.label: All other Greek lines · African Latin · Sinaitic Syriac · Coptic
A “Western” Greek copy
nodes.note: change triggered by v. 43, or a slip on a rare word

nodes.label: Syriac harmony tradition → Ephrem, sy-F
nodes.note: anger added beside the inherited compassion

explains: The shape of the tradition: one early strand against everything else.
Why the oldest Latin (e) and the Sinaitic Syriac have compassion.
Why the Syriac form is a double reading: compassion was already there when anger arrived.
Why anger appears in Latin and Syriac together, without any contact between them.
costs: It needs a reason for a scribe to turn compassion into anger. Proposals: the pull of ἐμβριμησάμενος in verse 43; “if you will” heard as an affront; an accidental swap of a rare word for a common look-alike.
None of these is as natural as the reverse change.
Matthew's silence at 8:3 needs explaining, since he usually keeps Mark's compassion.

holders.name: Bruce Metzger / UBS committee
holders.note: “Difficult to come to a firm decision”; swayed by the diversity and character of the evidence. Rated {B} since UBS4.

holders.name: Ernst Haenchen
holders.note: Unusual among commentators in arguing strongly for σπλαγχνισθείς (so France).

holders.name: Peter Head
holders.note: “Diverse and strong external attestation.”

holders.name: J. Donahue & D. Harrington
holders.note: Weight of the best manuscripts; anger left alone at 3:5 and 10:14; Jesus compassionate at 6:34, 8:2, 9:22.

holders.name: Adela Yarbro Collins
holders.note: Reads the scene as moving from pity (v. 41) to anger (v. 43).

holders.name: Peter J. Williams
holders.note: ὀργισθείς could arise from σπλαγχνισθείς “largely by accident”: same ending, a rare word replaced by the commonest -ισθείς form.

holders.name: NA28 / UBS5
holders.note: Print σπλαγχνισθείς.

holders.name: Tyndale House GNT
holders.note: Prints σπλαγχνισθείς.

holders.name: S. Kristianto
holders.note: Pre-genealogical coherence favours σπλαγχνισθείς.

holders.name: Editio Critica Maior, Mark
holders.note: Prints σπλαγχνισθείς with no split guiding line.

variants.title: Where Taylor 2020 fits
variants.text: D. G. K. Taylor does not decide which reading is original. His point is narrower and affects all three models: the Syriac evidence shows ὀργισθείς was a real Greek reading, not a Latin accident.

items.title: Anger arose in Latin; Bezae's Greek follows the Latin
items.short: No Greek ὀργισθείς ever existed before Bezae: iratus arose inside the Latin tradition and Bezae's Greek column was conformed to it.

nodes.label: The whole Greek tradition · Syriac · Coptic
Italian Old Latin (a, ff², r¹, d)
Bezae's Greek column
nodes.note: Greek conformed to a Latin model

nodes.label: Ephrem, sy-F
nodes.note: unexplained by this model: needs coincidence or Latin–Syriac contact

explains: Why no other Greek manuscript has ὀργισθείς.
Why the Latin witnesses to iratus belong to a single text-type and region.
Why the Latin tradition is so unsettled at this word: eight different forms and four verbs across eleven witnesses.
It matches a wider pattern: Lorenz counts 410 readings in Bezae's Mark that agree with the Latin against the Greek mainstream.
costs: The Syriac evidence. Ephrem and the Old Syriac palimpsest know “being angered” in a region with no Latin gospels.
The proposed Latin slip (autem misertus → autem iratus) does not fit: the anger manuscripts read Et iratus.
The direction of influence between Bezae's columns is disputed; Lorenz himself left it open in 2016.

holders.name: J. Rendel Harris
holders.note: An ambiguous Latin motus, later resolved as misertus or iratus, with Bezae's Greek retranslated.

holders.name: Peter J. Williams (blog)
holders.note: Suggested autem miser(a)tus → autem iratus; later preferred a Greek-internal accident.

holders.name: Jeff Cate
holders.note: Latin has no verb equivalent to σπλαγχνίζομαι; the variant “arose in Latin”.

holders.name: Peter Lorenz
holders.note: The anger witnesses reduce to one insular Latin tradition; “we are essentially counting the same Greek witness over and over.”

holders.name: James Snapp
holders.note: Bezae's Greek retranslated from Latin.

holders.name: Nathan Johnson
holders.note: “‘Anger’ originating in the Old Latin manuscript tradition”; the Syriac witness dismissed.

holders.name: Peter Lorenz (monograph)
holders.note: Bezae's Greek text of Mark was corrected towards a Latin model at the end of the fourth century.

variants.title: Written before the Syriac palimpsest was known
variants.text: Williams, Lorenz and Johnson all argued that support for anger comes exclusively from Latin-speaking areas. Taylor published the Old Syriac text in 2020.

arguments.intro: Each argument is given with the case for it, the replies, and where the reasoning currently stands. The markers show how each one bears on the three transmission models.

groups.title: External evidence
groups.question: What do the manuscripts and versions themselves tell us?

items.title: Compassion has the breadth
items.claim: σπλαγχνισθείς is read in every Greek text-form and in every ancient version.

pro.text: The UBS committee was moved by “the diversity and character of evidence”, not by numbers.
The oldest branch of each version where anger appears still has compassion: the African Latin (e) and the Sinaitic Syriac.
The Greek tradition shows no disturbance at this point — no marginal notes, corrections or mixed forms.

contra.text: Manuscripts must be weighed, not counted; slender support says nothing about a reading's merits.
A single early change, upstream of most surviving lines, would produce exactly this picture. Mark was little copied in the second century.

items.status: Strong, but not decisive on its own: it shows where the readings were, not which came first.

items.title: How many witnesses for anger are there really?
items.claim: The four Latin manuscripts and Bezae's Greek are not five witnesses but one tradition.

pro.text: Latin manuscripts that share a rendering go back to one translation and count once. The evidence “is equivalent to no more than two Greek witnesses”.
a, d, ff² and r¹ share one text-type, the “Western” gospel order and a northern Italian milieu of c. 350–380.

contra.text: Even on this count the reading reaches back before c. 350, earlier than any Greek manuscript of the verse except ℵ and B.
The Old Syriac palimpsest and Ephrem add a second, non-Latin region.

items.status: The Latin witnesses do collapse into one. The Syriac evidence, published later, is what keeps the anger reading from being purely local.

items.title: Is Bezae an independent Greek witness?
items.claim: Bezae's Greek text of Mark is late and mixed, and at this verse it may simply follow the Latin.

pro.text: Lorenz assigns 410 readings in Bezae's Mark to a “Latin layer”, 332 of them with no other Greek support; ὀργισθείς is in that list.
In the same clause Bezae reads αὐτοῦ ἥψατο αὐτοῦ, which combines the reading of ℵ B with the majority reading — a sign of a text that developed after both.
Bezae sides with ℵ B for καί at the start of the verse, then departs from all Greek manuscripts in the next word.

contra.text: Bezae preserves weakly attested original readings elsewhere in Mark, and 1:41 is one of them.
Readings of D supported by the Old Latin “are evidently part of a much older tradition” and should not be treated as singular.
Wholesale Latinization of Bezae's Greek is not accepted, though in places it remains the best explanation.
Bezae's scribe keeps σπλαγχνίζομαι in all eleven other Gospel occurrences (with several misspellings, e.g. ἐπλαννίσθη at Mark 6:34). The word was not being avoided.

items.status: Bezae on its own proves little either way. The case for an early Greek ὀργισθείς rests on the Latin–Syriac agreement, not on Bezae.

items.title: The Syriac evidence
items.claim: Ephrem and an Old Syriac manuscript attest “being angered” outside the Latin world.

pro.text: The palimpsest reads “had compassion on him and, being angered, stretched out his hand” — “precisely the double reading that Ephrem was attempting to explain”.
Ephrem cites the gospel word itself (“Our Lord was angry, therefore”); mistranslation in the standard editions hid this.
Agreements between Syriac and Old Latin against the Greek majority are best explained by “a lost common Greek reading”.

contra.text: Ephrem's anger word (root pwr) is not the usual Syriac equivalent of ὀργίζομαι.
Ephrem's talk of anger is anti-Marcionite rhetoric, not a citation. (Taylor: “a clever argument … quite implausible”.)
Ephrem's language “is fully accounted for by ἐμβριμησάμενος” in verse 43.
The Syriac form is a double reading. It presupposes a text with compassion and so is not evidence for anger instead of compassion.

items.status: This is the newest evidence and the least absorbed in the literature. One point is still open: how the palimpsest renders verse 43 has not been published, so it is not yet certain that “being angered” translates ὀργισθείς and not a displaced ἐμβριμησάμενος.

items.title: The witnesses that have neither word
items.claim: Some copies drop the participle altogether.

pro.text: The absence of either word in Old Latin b suggests a copyist found iratus and removed it.

contra.text: The Greek omitters are late Byzantine copies whose exemplars certainly read σπλαγχνισθείς; they are assimilating to Matthew and Luke.
If scribes were troubled by anger they would omit, as these do — not substitute a different emotion.
Minuscule 1358, often cited for ὀργισθείς, in fact omits.

items.status: Ambiguous. Only b is close enough to the anger witnesses for its silence to mean anything.

items.title: The Latin tradition is unsettled here
items.claim: Eleven Latin witnesses show eight different forms and four different verbs.

pro.text: Latin had no single verb for σπλαγχνίζομαι, so translators improvised — fertile ground for a stray rendering.

contra.text: The same variety could be successive corrections away from an inherited iratus: c and q may have been corrected to the Vulgate.

items.status: Shows that something happened in Latin, not what.

groups.title: What would scribes do?
groups.question: Which change is easier to imagine a copyist making?

items.title: The harder reading
items.claim: Scribes would turn anger into compassion, never the reverse.

pro.text: “Scribes might well have changed a statement that Jesus felt anger to one that he felt compassion, but it is difficult to see why they should have made the opposite change.”
The reading “is so striking and ‘improbable’ that a correction to the ‘safer’ σπλαγχνισθείς would be very natural”.

contra.text: Copyists left Jesus' anger at Mark 3:5 and his indignation at 10:14 alone.
Scribes sometimes added anger: Bezae and others insert ἐν ὀργῇ at Luke 6:10.
σπλαγχνίζομαι is rare outside the New Testament; linguistically it is the harder word.
Interpreters ancient and modern explain the anger so readily that its difficulty is “overstated”.

rejoinder.text: At 3:5 and 10:14 “there was obvious cause for anger”; here there is none, which is why only this one was changed.

items.status: The strongest single argument for anger, and the reason most commentators adopt it. No proposed route from compassion to anger is as natural.

items.title: An accidental swap in Greek
items.claim: ὀργισθείς replaced σπλαγχνισθείς by a copying slip.

pro.text: The words share their last six letters; ὀργισθείς is the commonest biblical form in -ισθείς, σπλαγχνισθείς a rarity.
If anger were original, it would be a remarkable coincidence that a substitute existed which is both a perfect contextual fit and graphically similar.
Bezae's own scribe stumbles over the word repeatedly: ἐπλαννίσθη (Mark 6:34), σπλαχνίζομαι (8:2), ἐσπλαγχίσθη (Luke 10:33).

contra.text: ΟΡΓ- is far shorter than ΣΠΛΑΓΧΝ-; the words do not look alike.
Proposals of accidental change are “unconvincing”.

items.status: Possible, not compelling. It supplies a mechanism for Model B without a motive.

items.title: Pulled in from verse 43
items.claim: Anger in verse 41 was suggested by ἐμβριμησάμενος two verses later.

pro.text: One of the origins the UBS committee considered.
Ephrem shows how an ancient reader got there: “in response to ‘if you will’ he was angered”.

contra.text: It does not explain why a copyist would act two verses early, replacing a word that made good sense.
The same link is used the other way: verse 43 shows the anger of verse 41 is at home in the story.

items.status: A real possibility that cuts both ways.

items.title: A confusion in Aramaic or Syriac
items.claim: ethraḥam (“he had pity”) and ethraʿem (“he was enraged”) differ by one guttural.

pro.text: Proposed by Zahn (Aramaic) and Rendel Harris (Syriac); listed by Metzger; still mentioned by Marcus.

contra.text: No Aramaic Mark is known to have existed.
The anger word the Syriac tradition actually has is mpār, not ethraʿem.

items.status: Now effectively ruled out by the Syriac evidence itself.

items.title: A slip in Latin
items.claim: iratus arose inside the Latin tradition.

pro.text: An ambiguous motus resolved two ways (Harris 1891); or autem miser(a)tus → autem iratus by loss of letters (Williams 2007).

contra.text: The anger manuscripts read Et iratus, not autem iratus; misertus goes with Iesus autem.
It cannot account for the Syriac.

items.status: The specific mechanisms proposed do not fit the Latin wording.

groups.title: Matthew and Luke
groups.question: The two earliest readers of Mark both have no emotion here. What does that show?

table.caption: What Matthew and Luke do with Mark's emotion words for Jesus

items.title: Both evangelists drop the word
items.claim: Matthew and Luke read ὀργισθείς in Mark and removed it, as they always remove Jesus' anger.

pro.text: “Matthew and Luke have no qualms about describing Jesus as compassionate. But they never describe him as angry … whenever Mark did so, they both rewrite the term out of their stories.”
If σπλαγχνισθείς were original they “would probably have included it”, since both use the term of Jesus elsewhere (Matt 9:36; Luke 7:13).

contra.text: Luke drops Mark's compassion at 9:11, so his silence here proves nothing.
Both also drop Jesus' love for the rich man (Mark 10:21): they remove warm emotions as well as harsh ones.
Both omit all of verse 43 too, and this pericope has a cluster of other Matthew–Luke agreements against Mark (ἥψατο αὐτοῦ λέγων, εὐθέως). The shared omission is part of a larger pattern.
The argument assumes Matthew and Luke edited Mark independently; if Luke knew Matthew, this is one agreement, not two.

items.status: Weaker than usually stated. Only Matthew's silence carries weight, and Matthew is abbreviating heavily here.

items.title: Matthew reuses the scene elsewhere
items.claim: Matthew's two healings of blind men borrow the vocabulary of Mark 1:41–45, including σπλαγχνισθείς.

pro.text: Matt 20:34 adds σπλαγχνισθεὶς … ἥψατο … εὐθέως to a Markan healing that has none of it — the same sequence as Mark 1:41–42.
Its doublet, Matt 9:30–31, has ἐνεβριμήθη, “see that no one knows” and διεφήμισαν — the vocabulary of Mark 1:43–45.

contra.text: σπλαγχνίζομαι is a favourite of Matthew's in any case (9:36; 18:27), so 20:34 need not depend on Mark 1:41.
Matthew “consistently keeps Markan ‘compassion’ language”, which makes its absence at 8:3 all the more striking.

items.status: Suggestive evidence that Matthew's copy of Mark had σπλαγχνισθείς.

groups.title: Mark's own story
groups.question: Which reading fits the passage and the Gospel?

items.title: The harshness of verse 43
items.claim: ἐμβριμησάμενος and ἐξέβαλεν show the scene is angry throughout.

pro.text: ἐμβριμάομαι is the snorting of a horse; of people, “to express indignation by an explosive expulsion of breath”. There is no reason to deny the nuance of anger here.
ἐξέβαλεν is the word used for casting out demons (1:34, 39).
The harsh words of v. 43 “cohere with the minority reading of v. 41”.

contra.text: The story can as well be read as a shift: pity in v. 41, stern dismissal in v. 43.
ἐκβάλλω is not always violent in Mark (1:12; 5:40).
The same harshness is what would lead a copyist to write anger in v. 41 (see “Pulled in from verse 43”).

items.status: Cuts both ways: coherence for one side, a source of contamination for the other.

items.title: Angry at what?
items.claim: If Jesus is angry, the text does not say why.

options.text: At the leper's “if you will”, as doubting his willingness
At the disease and the evil power behind it
At the purity system that excluded the man
At being asked to usurp the priest's role of declaring him clean
At the interruption of his preaching mission
It is the leper who is angry

pro.text: The lack of an obvious object is precisely what would provoke a correction.

contra.text: A reading that needs six competing explanations may simply be a mistake.
Or the reverse: if explanations come so easily, the reading was never very difficult.

items.status: No agreed answer among those who accept anger.

items.title: Mark's usage
items.claim: Both emotions are at home in Mark's portrait of Jesus.

pro.text: Compassion: 6:34; 8:2; 9:22 — NA28's own marginal references at 1:41.
Anger and indignation: 3:5; 10:14. Mark's Jesus also sighs (7:34; 8:12) and is distressed (14:33).

items.status: Mark's style does not decide the question.

positions.intro: Critical editions mostly print compassion; commentators mostly argue for anger; the specialist text-critical articles of 2012–2018 mostly defend compassion.

items.name: NET (current)
items.note: “Moved with indignation”; the first edition read compassion

items.name: Beavis (Paideia)
items.note: presents both; notes v. 43 coheres with anger

items.claim: “Minuscule 1358 reads ὀργισθείς.”
items.fact: It omits the word. The citation is an error in Text und Textwert (1998), corrected by Cate in 2011.

items.claim: “Anger is supported only in Latin-speaking areas.”
items.fact: Ephrem and the Old Syriac palimpsest (published 2020) attest it in Syria.

items.claim: “Ephrem read anger instead of compassion.”
items.fact: His text, like the palimpsest, had both.

items.claim: “Four or five independent witnesses support anger.”
items.fact: The Latin manuscripts are one text-type; Bezae's Greek may depend on it.

items.claim: “The UBS committee simply followed the majority.”
items.fact: Metzger cites the diversity and character of the evidence, not its quantity.

items.claim: “The UBS rating is {D}.”
items.fact: That was UBS3. It has been {B} since UBS4.

items.claim: “Many manuscripts read compassion” (NIV footnote).
“iratus came from autem misertus by a copying slip.”
items.fact: The manuscripts with iratus read Et iratus.

items.claim: “Lake argued for an angry Jesus.”
items.fact: He made the leper the subject of ὀργισθείς.

assessment.title: One reading of the evidence
assessment.label: A provisional judgment, offered for discussion
paragraphs: “Only in Bezae” is the wrong frame. Bezae itself is weak evidence: its Greek text at this verse is late and mixed. But the reading it carries is old. Latin Italy and Syriac-speaking Mesopotamia both know it by the mid-fourth century, and the cheapest link between them is a second-century Greek text.

That makes the real question a general one: how often does a single early “Western” strand preserve the original against everything else? The internal arguments do not settle it. The harder-reading argument is real, but the synoptic argument is weaker than it looks, and the Syriac form is a double reading that presupposes compassion beside it.
On balance σπλαγχνισθείς is the more probable original — roughly two to one — with ὀργισθείς an early and respectable rival, not a scribal curiosity.
openQuestions: How does the Old Syriac palimpsest render verse 43? If its “being angered” is a displaced ἐμβριμησάμενος, the Syriac ceases to be evidence for ὀργισθείς.
What does Bruehler (2025) make of the Syriac evidence and of Lorenz's monograph?
What do the coherence data for this variation unit in the ECM of Mark show?
